title: Two Ways to Mend a Broken Chromosome

scenes.tts: The first film followed repair while one strand still held a usable partner. What can a cell do when a break cuts both strands? The blue chromosome now separates into two ends. No continuous partner crosses the gap. The cell can work with those ends, or search for matching DNA elsewhere.

scenes.visual: Open on the first film's two thick blue rows already filling the frame. A red flash cuts across both rows; the left and right pieces drift apart. The gold partner highlight stops at the gap, and a red question mark expands between the ends. Add two moving arrows: one curves the ends together, and one searches outward. Mark the chromosome picture 'schematic'.

scenes.visual: Without clearing the break, slide the two ends outward to frame the title 'Two Ways to Mend a Broken Chromosome'. Keep the first film's color map: blue DNA, red damage, gold trusted template, green restored DNA, teal repair machinery.

scenes.tts: A broken chromosome can join its ends or copy a matching template. Non-homologous end joining chooses the ends already present. Homologous recombination copies a matching template, usually the sister chromatid. Neither name guarantees one outcome. The ends' condition and the available template shape what happens next.

scenes.visual: Carry the same broken blue chromosome into a forked path. On the left, the two ends curve toward each other under 'join ends'. On the right, a gold chromosome track glides behind the gap under 'copy a template'. Do not label either branch accurate or error-prone. A teal selector moves between paths.

scenes.tts: Start with end joining. Teal Ku rings grip both blue ends and recruit partners that hold them together. Clean, compatible ends may be joined without changing their sequence. Ends that do not fit need trimming or filling before ligation. That processing can remove or add bases, so accuracy depends on the break.

scenes.visual: Zoom into the left branch. Two thick teal cuffs labeled 'Ku' slide over the blue ends; smaller teal partner shapes arrive and bridge the two cuffs, bringing compatible block edges together. First show a clean join turning green. Reset to ragged red tips; teal tools trim one tip and add one plain block to the other before a green joint forms. Label both outcomes 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: End joining needs no matching template. It can therefore operate throughout the cell cycle. Before DNA replication, that matters because no sister chromatid exists. After replication, another option becomes available beside it.

scenes.visual: Pull back to a horizontal cell-cycle strip with a single blue chromosome moving from 'before replication' to 'during and after replication'. Teal Ku cuffs travel beneath the entire strip. A faint gold sister track begins only after the replication boundary and slowly brightens.

scenes.tts: Here are two cells, one before replication and one after. Which cell can copy from a sister chromatid? Watch where you expect a matching gold chromosome to appear.

scenes.visual: Show two large cells side by side. The left contains one broken blue chromosome; the right contains the same broken blue chromosome. Put an empty gold outline in each cell and a moving question mark above them. On-screen question: 'Where is a sister available?'

scenes.visual: Hold both cells and the question. Let the empty gold outlines pulse gently, but reveal no sister and no answer during the pause.

scenes.tts: After replication, each chromosome has a sister chromatid. That matching copy makes homologous recombination useful during and after replication. The broken blue chromosome aligns beside the gold sister. Before replication, the sister is absent, so this sister-templated route is unavailable.

In the left cell, collapse the empty gold outline into the label 'no sister yet'. Keep teal end-joining cuffs visible in both cells so the picture does not imply end joining stops after replication.

scenes.tts: Homologous recombination first reshapes the break into single-stranded tails. A recombinase coats a tail and helps it search the gold sister. At matching DNA, the tail invades. Its end primes new green DNA, copying information from the intact template. The repaired chromosome keeps the sister's sequence across the gap.

scenes.visual: Zoom into the right cell. Taper the broken blue ends into single-stranded tails without molecular detail. Teal beads labeled 'recombinase' coat one tail. The tail scans along the gold sister, pauses at a matching block pattern, and tucks beside it. A green track grows from the blue tail while a gold guide highlight advances underneath.

scenes.tts: Copying does not force a crossover. Often the extended strand leaves the donor and pairs with the other broken end. Another branch can form crossed junctions before separation. Both begin by using matching DNA as information.

scenes.visual: From the copied green stretch, branch the animation without changing camera. In the upper route, the extended blue-green strand lifts away from gold and pairs with its other blue end. In the lower route, blue and gold tracks form two simple crossed junction icons labeled 'crossed junctions, schematic'. Do not show molecular geometry or imply every event crosses over.

scenes.tts: Reset the same break. End joining preserves clean compatible ends, but processing may change them. Homologous recombination can restore missing sequence from a sister, but only when that template exists. The choice is not a contest between bad and good repair. It responds to available information and cell-cycle context.

scenes.tts: When both strands break, ask what remains. Are two joinable ends the only local evidence? Is an intact sister nearby to copy? Those questions predict the route and its possible outcome.

Both brackets transform into the centered prompt 'What information remains?' while the repaired chromosome moves slowly beneath it.
